name: Springs in Series — Equivalent Stiffness
description: Computes the equivalent stiffness of two springs connected in series. It is the reciprocal of the sum of the individual compliances (1/k1 + 1/k2), so the springs share the same force while their deflections add.
notes: The combined stiffness is always lower than either spring alone. For springs in parallel the rates simply add instead. All rates must use the same units.

name: Springs in Parallel — Equivalent Stiffness
description: Computes the equivalent stiffness of two springs connected in parallel by simply adding their rates k1 and k2. In parallel the springs share the same deflection while their forces add.
notes: The combined stiffness is always higher than either spring alone. This is the opposite of the series case, where compliances add. All rates must use the same units.

name: Bearing Life in Hours (L10h)
description: Estimates the L10 rating life of a rolling bearing in operating hours. It raises the ratio of dynamic load rating C to equivalent load P to the life exponent, gives millions of revolutions, then converts using speed N in rpm.
notes: L10 means 90 percent of bearings survive at least this long. Use pp=3 for ball bearings and 10/3 for roller bearings. C and P must be in the same units and N in rpm.

name: Modified Goodman Allowable Alternating Stress
description: Computes the allowable alternating stress under a given mean stress using the modified Goodman fatigue criterion. It reduces the endurance limit se linearly by the fraction of mean stress sm to ultimate strength su.
notes: The Goodman line uses ultimate strength su as the mean-stress intercept, giving a conservative safe boundary. Requires sm less than su; at sm equal to su the allowable alternating stress reaches zero.

name: Soderberg Allowable Alternating Stress
description: Computes the allowable alternating stress under a mean stress using the Soderberg fatigue criterion. It reduces the endurance limit se linearly by the ratio of mean stress sm to yield strength sy.
notes: The Soderberg line uses yield strength sy as the intercept, making it more conservative than Goodman by guarding against yielding as well as fatigue. Requires sm less than sy.

name: Gerber Allowable Alternating Stress
description: Computes the allowable alternating stress under a mean stress using the Gerber parabolic fatigue criterion. It reduces the endurance limit se by one minus the square of the ratio of mean stress sm to ultimate strength su.
notes: The Gerber parabola fits fatigue data better than the linear Goodman line and is less conservative. Requires sm less than su; the mean-stress term is squared, unlike Goodman's linear term.

name: Marin Corrected Endurance Limit
description: Computes a corrected endurance limit by applying Marin modifying factors to the rotary-beam (specimen) endurance limit sep. Here it multiplies the surface, size, and load factors together with sep.
notes: Each Marin factor is a dimensionless value at or below 1 that de-rates the ideal specimen limit for real conditions. A full analysis may include further factors for temperature and reliability.

name: Peak Stress from Stress-Concentration Factor
description: Computes the peak local stress at a geometric discontinuity by multiplying the nominal stress snom by the stress-concentration factor Kt. It captures how features like holes or fillets amplify stress locally.
notes: Kt is the theoretical (elastic) factor and applies while the material stays elastic. Under fatigue a notch factor Kf, usually smaller than Kt, is used instead. snom is the stress on the net section.

name: Flywheel Inertia from Coefficient of Fluctuation
description: Computes the mass moment of inertia a flywheel needs to hold speed variation within a target coefficient of fluctuation Cs. It equals the energy fluctuation Ee divided by Cs times the mean angular speed omega squared.
notes: Cs is the allowable fractional speed swing (dimensionless); a smoother machine needs a smaller Cs and hence larger inertia. omega is the mean angular speed in rad/s, and Ee is the energy swing per cycle.

name: Belt Friction Tension Ratio (Euler)
description: Computes the ratio of tight-side to slack-side tension for a belt about to slip on a pulley, from the Euler-Eytelwein capstan equation. It equals e raised to the friction coefficient mu times the wrap angle theta.
notes: theta is the wrap (contact) angle in radians, not degrees. Gives the maximum ratio at the point of impending slip; actual ratios are lower. For V-belts an effective friction coefficient is used.

name: Belt Power Transmitted
description: Computes the power transmitted by a belt drive. It equals the difference between the tight-side tension T1 and slack-side tension T2, multiplied by the belt speed v.
notes: T1 minus T2 is the net driving (effective) tension. Belt speed v is in m/s, giving power in watts. Ignores centrifugal-tension effects, which reduce transmissible power at high speeds.

name: Centrifugal Tension in Belt
description: Computes the centrifugal tension induced in a moving belt by the inertia of its own mass. It equals the mass per unit length times the belt speed v squared, and adds to the belt tension on both sides.
notes: Rises with the square of belt speed, becoming significant at high speeds and reducing the tension available for power transmission. Mass per length is in kg/m and v in m/s.

name: Hydraulic Cylinder Force (Extension)
description: Computes the pushing force a hydraulic cylinder produces on extension. It equals the supply pressure p times the full bore area (pi times bore diameter D squared over 4), since the whole piston face is pressurized.
notes: Uses the full bore diameter, valid for the extend stroke; the retract stroke acts on the smaller rod-side annular area. p is gauge pressure. Ignores seal friction and back-pressure losses.

name: Hydraulic Cylinder Force (Rod Side)
description: Computes the pulling force a hydraulic cylinder produces on the rod side during retraction. It equals the supply pressure p times the annular area, pi times the difference of bore diameter D squared and rod diameter d squared over 4.
notes: The rod displaces part of the piston area, so this retract force is less than the extend force. D and d are diameters. p is gauge pressure; seal friction and losses are ignored.

name: Lewis Bending Stress (Gear Tooth)
description: Estimates the bending stress at the root of a gear tooth using the Lewis equation. It divides the tangential force Ft by the product of face width fw, module mo, and the Lewis form factor Yl, treating the tooth as a cantilever.
notes: Yl depends on tooth count and pressure angle. This is a static estimate; real designs add a dynamic factor for speed and stress-concentration effects at the fillet. Module mo is here in metres.

name: Sommerfeld Number (Journal Bearing)
description: Computes the Sommerfeld number, a dimensionless characteristic of a journal bearing. It multiplies the square of the radius-to-clearance ratio (r/c) by the viscosity mu times speed N over the bearing pressure P.
notes: N is rotational speed in rev/s and P is the projected bearing pressure (load over projected area). This dimensionless group sets the bearing's operating regime and correlates friction and minimum film thickness.

name: Petroff Bearing Friction Torque
expression: 4 * pi^2 * mu * N * L * r^3 / c
description: Estimates the friction torque of a lightly loaded journal bearing using Petroff's equation. It scales with viscosity mu, speed N, bearing length L, and the cube of journal radius r, divided by the radial clearance c.
notes: Valid for a concentric, lightly loaded bearing with a full oil film. N is in rev/s. Torque rises steeply with radius (cube) and falls as clearance increases; it ignores eccentricity effects.

name: Disc Clutch Torque (Uniform Wear)
description: Computes the torque a disc clutch or brake can transmit under the uniform-wear assumption. It equals half the friction coefficient mu times axial force F times the number of friction surfaces z times the sum of outer and inner radii.
notes: Uniform-wear theory uses the mean radius (ro+ri)/2 and gives a lower, more conservative torque than the uniform-pressure model. z counts the friction interfaces, not the discs.

name: Disc Clutch Torque (Uniform Pressure)
description: Computes the torque a disc clutch or brake can transmit under the uniform-pressure assumption. It uses two-thirds of the friction coefficient mu times axial force F and surfaces z, times the ratio of the radii-cubed difference to the radii-squared difference.
notes: Uniform-pressure theory applies to new, unworn surfaces and gives a higher torque than the uniform-wear model. z is the number of friction interfaces; the radius ratio is the effective friction radius.

name: Critical (Whirling) Speed of Shaft
description: Gives the critical (whirling) rotational speed of a shaft in rpm, at which centrifugal effects resonate with the shaft's lateral vibration. It is found from the gravitational acceleration divided by the static deflection the load causes, so a stiffer shaft with smaller deflection spins faster before whirling.
notes: Static deflection must be in metres; a very small deflection gives a very high speed. Operating near this speed causes dangerous whirl, so shafts run well below or above it. Assumes a single-mass model.

name: Torsional Natural Frequency
description: Calculates the natural frequency of a torsional (rotary) vibrating system in hertz from its torsional stiffness and mass moment of inertia. It is the square root of stiffness over inertia divided by 2 pi (tau), so a stiffer shaft or lighter rotor vibrates faster.
notes: Here tau denotes 2 pi, converting angular frequency to cycles per second. Stiffness is torque per radian and inertia is the rotational (not linear) mass property; do not confuse it with linear mass.

name: Damped Natural Frequency
description: Gives the damped natural frequency of a vibrating system: the frequency at which it actually oscillates once damping is present. It equals the undamped frequency times the square root of one minus the damping ratio squared, so damping lowers the oscillation frequency.
notes: Valid only for underdamped systems with damping ratio below 1; at or above 1 the term under the root is zero or negative and no oscillation occurs. Damping ratio is dimensionless.

name: Logarithmic Decrement
description: Computes the logarithmic decrement, the natural log of the ratio of successive amplitude peaks in a decaying free vibration. It equals 2 pi (tau) times the damping ratio over the square root of one minus the damping ratio squared, quantifying how fast oscillations die out.
notes: Here tau denotes 2 pi. Valid for underdamped systems (damping ratio below 1). For light damping it is approximately 2 pi times the damping ratio; the exact form is used here.

name: Half-Power Bandwidth
description: Estimates the half-power (3 dB) bandwidth of a resonant peak as twice the damping ratio times the natural frequency. This width between the half-power points is used to identify damping from a measured frequency-response curve.
notes: This 2 zeta wn approximation holds only for light damping (small damping ratio). Natural frequency is in rad/s, so the result is a bandwidth in rad/s, not hertz.

name: Damping Ratio (Zeta)
description: Calculates the dimensionless damping ratio of a single-degree-of-freedom system from its damping coefficient, stiffness and mass. It is the actual damping divided by the critical damping 2 times the square root of stiffness times mass, indicating how the system decays.
notes: A value below 1 is underdamped (oscillates), 1 is critically damped, above 1 is overdamped. Use consistent SI units; the denominator is the critical damping coefficient.

name: Gyroscopic Couple
description: Gives the gyroscopic couple (reaction moment) produced when a spinning rotor is forced to precess. It is the product of the rotor's moment of inertia, its spin speed and the precession rate, and acts perpendicular to both the spin and precession axes.
notes: Both spin and precession rates must be in rad/s. The couple acts about an axis perpendicular to the plane of spin and precession; convert rpm to rad/s before use.

name: Reciprocating Engine Piston Acceleration
description: Approximates the acceleration of a reciprocating engine piston as crank radius times crank angular speed squared times cosine of the crank angle plus cosine of twice the angle divided by the rod-to-crank ratio. The two cosine terms are the primary and secondary inertia effects.
notes: Crank angle must be in radians. This is the standard slider-crank approximation valid for moderate rod ratios; the second term captures the secondary (2 theta) unbalance ignored by a simple sinusoid.

name: Wahl Correction Factor (Helical Spring)
description: Computes the Wahl correction factor for a helical compression spring, which scales the nominal shear stress to account for curvature and the direct shear stress. It depends only on the spring index (coil-to-wire diameter ratio); tighter coils give a larger factor.
notes: Spring index is dimensionless (mean coil diameter over wire diameter) and is typically between 4 and 12. Smaller indices give sharply higher factors, so very tight coils are avoided.

name: Gear Pitch-Line Velocity
description: Gives the pitch-line velocity of a gear, the linear speed at its pitch circle, as pi times the pitch diameter times the rotational speed in rpm divided by 60. This velocity governs dynamic loads and lubrication requirements in gear design.
notes: Pitch diameter is in metres and speed in rpm; the 60 converts rpm to rev/s. The result is the tangential speed at the pitch circle, not the shaft surface speed.

name: Bolt Preload from Tightening Torque
description: Estimates the axial preload (clamping force) developed in a bolt from the applied tightening torque, using the torque divided by the nut factor times the bolt diameter. It is the everyday relation linking wrench torque to bolt tension.
notes: The nut factor lumps thread and head friction and varies widely with lubrication and finish, so preload estimates carry large scatter. Bolt diameter is the nominal diameter in metres.

name: Rolling Resistance Force
description: Gives the rolling resistance force opposing a rolling wheel or tyre as the rolling resistance coefficient times the normal load pressing the wheel to the surface. It represents the energy lost to deformation as the wheel rolls.
notes: The coefficient is dimensionless and depends on tyre, surface and inflation. Normal load is the perpendicular force in newtons, not the vehicle weight if the load is shared among wheels.

name: Equivalent Dynamic Bearing Load
description: Computes the equivalent dynamic load on a rolling bearing that combines radial and axial loads into a single value, as the radial factor times radial load plus the axial factor times axial load. This equivalent load is used in bearing life calculations.
notes: The radial and axial factors X and Y come from bearing catalogues and depend on the load ratio and bearing type; the values here are illustrative defaults, not universal.

name: Power Screw Torque to Raise Load
expression: F * dm / 2 * (lead + pi * mu * dm) / (pi * dm - mu * lead)
description: Gives the torque needed to raise an axial load with a power (lead) screw, accounting for thread friction. It uses the load times half the mean diameter times the ratio combining lead, friction coefficient and mean diameter, capturing both lifting work and friction losses.
notes: Mean diameter and lead must be in metres. This covers thread friction only; add collar or bearing friction separately. Uses a square-thread model, so trapezoidal threads need a friction adjustment.

name: Power Screw Efficiency
expression: lead / (pi * dm) * (pi * dm - mu * lead) / (lead + pi * mu * dm)
description: Calculates the efficiency of a power (lead) screw as the ratio of useful lifting work to input work, from the lead, mean diameter and friction coefficient. It shows what fraction of the applied torque actually raises the load rather than overcoming friction.
notes: Lead and mean diameter must share units (metres here). Result is a fraction between 0 and 1; higher lead and lower friction raise efficiency. Covers thread friction only, not collar friction.

name: Coefficient of Fluctuation of Speed
description: Gives the coefficient of fluctuation of speed for a rotating machine, the difference between maximum and minimum angular speeds divided by the mean speed. It measures how uneven the running speed is over a cycle, guiding flywheel sizing.
notes: All three speeds share the same units, so the result is dimensionless. A smaller coefficient means smoother running; it is set by the required flywheel inertia.

name: Cam Follower Maximum Velocity (SHM)
description: Gives the maximum velocity of a cam follower moving with simple harmonic motion during rise, as pi times the lift times the cam angular speed divided by twice the rise angle. The peak occurs at mid-lift.
notes: Rise angle beta must be in radians and cam speed in rad/s. This assumes an SHM cam profile; other profiles (cycloidal, polynomial) give different peak velocities.

name: Cam Follower Maximum Acceleration (SHM)
description: Gives the maximum acceleration of a cam follower under simple harmonic motion, as pi squared times the lift times the cam angular speed squared divided by twice the rise angle squared. Peaks occur at the start and end of the rise.
notes: Rise angle must be in radians and cam speed in rad/s. SHM motion has finite but abrupt acceleration steps at the ends, causing jerk; smoother profiles are preferred at high speed.

name: Reynolds Number (Lubrication Film)
description: Computes the Reynolds number of a lubricating oil film as oil density times surface speed times film thickness divided by oil viscosity. This dimensionless ratio of inertial to viscous forces indicates whether the film flow stays laminar.
notes: Use consistent SI units so the result is dimensionless; viscosity here is dynamic (Pa s). In hydrodynamic bearings the film Reynolds number is normally very small, confirming laminar flow.

name: Force Transmissibility Ratio
description: Gives the force transmissibility of a damped single-degree-of-freedom isolator, the ratio of force transmitted to the base versus the applied force, as a function of damping ratio and frequency ratio. It shows how well vibration isolation performs.
notes: Frequency ratio is the forcing frequency over the natural frequency. Isolation (ratio below 1) requires a frequency ratio above the square root of 2; more damping helps near resonance but worsens high-frequency isolation.

name: Rotational Kinetic Energy of Flywheel
description: Gives the rotational kinetic energy stored in a flywheel as one half the moment of inertia times the angular speed squared. This is the energy available to smooth out speed fluctuations in machinery.
notes: Angular speed must be in rad/s; energy rises with its square, so speed matters far more than inertia. Moment of inertia is the rotational property in kg m squared.

name: Gear Module (Pitch Diameter / Teeth)
description: Gives the module of a spur gear, a basic size parameter, as the pitch diameter divided by the number of teeth. The module sets the tooth size and must match between meshing gears.
notes: Pitch diameter here is in metres, so the module is in metres; module is more commonly quoted in millimetres. Mating gears must share the same module to mesh correctly.

name: Involute Function
description: Evaluates the involute function of an angle, defined as the tangent of the pressure angle minus the angle itself. This function is central to involute gear tooth geometry and to locating points along an involute curve.
notes: The angle must be in radians, and tangent minus angle is a small difference, so precision matters near small angles. Defined for pressure angles below pi/2 where the tangent is finite.

name: Collar Thrust Bearing Friction Torque (Uniform Wear)
description: Gives the friction torque of a flat collar thrust bearing under the uniform-wear assumption, as half the friction coefficient times the axial thrust times the sum of outer and inner radii. It represents the torque lost to friction at the collar face.
notes: Uses the uniform-wear model, which gives a slightly lower torque than the uniform-pressure model. Radii are in metres; the mean friction radius is the average of the two radii.

name: Mechanical Power from Torque and Angular Velocity
description: Computes the mechanical power transmitted by a rotating shaft as torque T times angular velocity omega. This is the direct SI form of the power-torque-speed relationship.
notes: Angular velocity omega must be in rad/s, not rpm. This library also has RPM-based torque-power formulas elsewhere that include the 2·pi/60 conversion factor; use this SI/direct form only when omega is already in rad/s.

name: Mechanical Efficiency
description: Computes the mechanical efficiency of a machine as the ratio of power output to power input, expressed as a percentage.
notes: Efficiency is always below 100% for real machines because of friction and other losses. Pout and Pin must be measured in the same power unit.

name: Construction Equipment Hourly Output
description: Estimates the hourly production rate of earthmoving equipment such as excavators or loaders from the load capacity per cycle q, a soil/material conversion factor f, a work efficiency factor Ew, and the cycle time Cm in minutes.
notes: Ew accounts for operator skill, job-site conditions, and management delays (typically 0.5-0.9); f converts between bank, loose, and compacted volume states. This is the standard production-rate formula used in earthmoving equipment estimating.
